scenes.heading: HTL / Sightly (Part 1 of 2)
scenes.narration: Code Quality. HTL / Sightly (Part 1 of 2). In this video we review 6 key concepts you need to know for the certification.

scenes.question: HTL-001 (Severity: Major) flags the use of context='unsafe' in HTL expressions. What does this context option do and why is it prohibited?
scenes.heading: context='unsafe' disables all HTL XSS escaping — output is inserted into the DOM raw and unescaped, enabling XSS attacks
scenes.body: HTL-001 (Major): HTL's primary security feature is automatic output escaping. Every '${expression}' is HTML-escaped by default. Using context='unsafe' removes this protection completely: the raw value is written directly into the HTML output. If the value contains '<script>alert(1)</script>', this executes as JavaScript in the victim's browser — a stored or reflected XSS vulnerability.

scenes.question: When is context='html' the correct HTL output context to use, and what security mechanism does HTL still apply?
scenes.heading: Use context='html' only for trusted, pre-validated rich text from the CMS RTE — HTL applies Anti-Samy sanitization to remove dangerous tags/attributes
scenes.body: HTL-001 and security: context='html' is the correct context for HTML-formatted rich text from the CMS RTE (Rich Text Editor). Unlike context='unsafe' (no protection), context='html' runs the value through Adobe's Anti-Samy HTML whitelist sanitizer, which strips dangerous elements (script, object, embed) and event handler attributes (onclick, onerror) while preserving safe formatting tags. Never use context='html' for user-submitted form data.

scenes.question: HTL-002 (Severity: Major) requires using data-sly-use to bind Java Sling Models or WCMUsePojo for business logic. Why does data-sly-use enforce this separation?
scenes.heading: data-sly-use delegates business logic to Java/JS Use-API objects while keeping HTL purely declarative — no JSP-style scriptlets
scenes.body: HTL-002 (Major): HTL was designed as a template language with intentionally limited expressiveness — it cannot execute arbitrary Java or perform complex computations inline. data-sly-use.model='com.myproject.MyModel' injects a Java Use-API object into the template, providing access to pre-computed properties. This enforces MVC separation: the @Model handles all data preparation and business logic; the HTL file handles only presentation.

scenes.question: Which HTL attribute causes its element and all its children to be removed from the DOM output if the condition expression evaluates to false?
scenes.heading: data-sly-test
scenes.body: HTL conditional rendering uses data-sly-test. When '${myModel.showSection}' is false/null/empty, the element with data-sly-test and its entire subtree are suppressed from the output. Falsy values are: false, null, 0, empty string, empty array/collection. This is roughly equivalent to JSP's <c:if test='...'> but more readable and type-safe.

scenes.question: What does the 'data-sly-unwrap' HTL attribute do to the element it is placed on?
scenes.heading: It renders the element's children while removing the element's own start and end tags from the output

scenes.question: HTL-004 requires the correct output context for expressions placed inside a JavaScript event handler attribute (e.g., onclick). Which context should be used?
scenes.heading: context='scriptToken' for safe identifier values, or context='scriptString' for string values — never 'unsafe' for inline JS
scenes.body: HTL-004 (Major): Expression output context must match the syntactic context it appears in. For inline JavaScript, incorrect escaping can create XSS vulnerabilities. HTL provides: context='scriptToken' for values used as JS identifiers or numbers (allows only safe characters), and context='scriptString' for values embedded inside JS string literals (applies JS string escaping with \u encoding). The default HTML attribute escaping does not protect against JavaScript injection within event handlers.
